extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, journalism students, newsroom editors and journalists, media researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and empirical criteria for identifying what makes an event or story 'news' in mainstream UK journalism (and how these values may have changed in the digital/social-media era). Used for content analysis and for guiding newsroom selection decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power elite (NV1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More significant in broadsheet/quality press; can include large corporations as part of this category; indicates stories about those with political, economic or institutional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity (NV2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning people who are already famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially prominent in red-top tabloids and popular press; celebrity may also appear in quality titles but to a lesser extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment (NV3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning sex, showbusiness, human interest, animals, an unfolding drama, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, entertaining photographs or witty headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue this broad category can be usefully split (e.g., drama; sport; showbusiness). Entertainment has both a 'dark' and 'light' side (e.g., grim human-interest vs. light jokey pieces); common in popular and mid-market titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (NV4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that have an element of surprise and/or contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should explicitly include 'unusualness' within its definition; surprise ranked highly in empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news (NV5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly negative overtones, such as conflict or tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad news is the most frequent news value in the sample; authors note a case for separating 'conflict' out from this broad category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news (NV6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly positive overtones, such as rescues and cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less frequent than bad news but still significant; stories can simultaneously be coded as both good and bad depending on perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (NV7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are perceived as sufficiently significant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest magnitude should also cover extreme behaviours or occurrences (not just large numbers), e.g., particularly gruesome or extreme events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance (NV8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about issues, groups and nations perceived to be relevant to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience relevance is a key criterion and varies between audiences and outlets (local proximity example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up (NV9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about subjects already in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes continuing coverage and developments of ongoing stories; news organisations commonly give prominence to follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper agenda (NV10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit the news organisation’s own agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be overt (editorial stance) or subtle; some titles show stronger agenda-driven selection; agendas influence framing and whether issues are emphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity / Being first
rubrics_metrics.description: Being the first to report a story or having exclusive material (an investigation, poll, or scoop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusivity often increases news value and can override other values (e.g., timeliness); newspapers frequently highlight exclusives in headlines and leads; suggested by authors to be a separate news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Recency and being current/first with a story; topicality of the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz and Brighton & Foy identify timeliness/topicality as dominant factors; in rolling/online news timeliness often interacts with exclusivity and competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that allow audience identification with characters, victims or situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz lists identification among dominant news values; identification can increase audience engagement and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving disagreement, confrontation or struggle between actors or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips (2015) argues conflict should be treated as a distinct news value (not merely a subset of 'bad news'); conflict appears frequently and drives audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation / Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with sensational qualities intended to provoke strong emotions or shock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz lists 'sensation'; Allern's commercial news values note sensationalist stories are more likely to be pursued; often tied to commercial pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement and presentation of the story (structure, format, design choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy include composition as a factor; composition interacts with how a story is presented and can affect perceived newsworthiness (e.g., layout, headlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: How a story conforms to or defies audience and newsroom expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy include expectation; expectation influences surprise value and editorial judgments about prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an event is out of the ordinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy list unusualness; authors suggest this concept be folded explicitly into 'surprise' but it is often treated separately in other taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived worthiness of a story in terms of importance or value to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy list worth as a consideration; worth may incorporate civic importance or human-interest value.

rubrics_metrics.name: External influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences on news selection from external actors such as public relations professionals, proprietors, advertisers and other actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy and multiple authors stress external influences (PR, spin, proprietorial pressure) shape selection; 'news subsidies' from PR increase uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Market-driven criteria affecting selection: sensational stories prioritized; expensive stories less likely; stories aided by news subsidies more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allern proposes this supplementary set: newsrooms favour sensational/cheap-to-produce items and rely on press releases, photo opportunities and prepared material (prefabrication).

rubrics_metrics.name: News subsidy / Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Material provided by outside actors (press releases, photo ops) that reduces newsroom costs and increases uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'news subsidy' or 'prefabrication' (Bell 1991); especially used by resource-constrained newsrooms; increases likelihood of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visuals / Strong imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence and strength of photographs, graphics or other visual elements that make a story more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caple and Bednarek (2015) and the authors note visuals can convey and emphasise news values (bad news, drama, surprise) and are especially important for shareability on social platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability / Sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualities of a story that make it likely to be shared on social media (Facebook, Twitter), influencing editorial selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors identify 'shareability' as a contemporary news value; Janine Gibson notes most shared stories 'make you laugh' or 'make you angry'; Facebook favors accessible, entertainment/lifestyle content; social metrics can shape newsroom priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience metrics / Clicks / Traffic
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative audience signals (clicks, shares, likes, tweets) that influence which stories are selected and promoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies cited show clicks and shares affect editorial decisions; editors monitor social feedback and audience behavior when deciding prominence and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-generated content / Participatory contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Material supplied or circulated by audiences (UGC) that can be used in news production and affect news selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note UGC has increased in importance for selection and dissemination, though it is more prominent in tabloid/online popular content than in hard news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of news values per story
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that single stories often satisfy multiple news values simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The taxonomy is not mutually exclusive — stories can be coded against several values (e.g., both bad and good news; surprise and magnitude); interaction effects between values are analytically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological coding reliability (procedural guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying a news-values taxonomy to content analysis, coding should be done by multiple coders with consensus discussions to manage subjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors double-coded every story and discussed discrepancies to reach consensus; they acknowledge subjectivity but argue large samples mitigate individual bias.
